analysis.one_liner: Charges oil and gas companies a fee on methane they release into the air, funding coastal protection grants.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees and their subcommittees until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Department to measure, basin by basin, how much methane each oil and gas basin leaks into the atmosphere, and to charge companies a fee starting at $1,800 per ton on the emissions that exceed a small allowance — 0.2% of what they produce, 0.1% for pipelines and processors [S3]. Companies could escape most of the fee by adopting independently validated, publicly reported leak-detection programs and stopping routine venting and flaring [S3]. All the fee money would go to grants for coastal resilience projects through the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation [S2]. It died without any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in coastal communities that flood, since the fee revenue would fund resilience grants; everyone exposed to climate damage, since methane is a potent heat-trapping gas and the bill's own findings call it responsible for roughly a quarter of observed warming [S3]; and energy consumers indirectly, because captured methane is marketable gas — the bill's findings estimate U.S. oil and gas operations vent about $2 billion of natural gas a year, enough to heat 10 million homes [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and anyone exposed to climate risk

how_it_helps.text: Starts at $1,800 per ton in 2023 and rises 2% a year plus inflation, giving companies a direct financial reason to find and fix leaks rather than vent gas into the air [S3].

Applies only to methane wasted above 0.2% of production (0.1% for gathering, processing, and transmission), so companies that simply stop wasting gas pay little or nothing — the bill's findings cite IEA estimates that half of oil and gas methane emissions could be eliminated at zero net cost [S3].
Routes every dollar of the fee to coastal resilience grants through the National Coastal Resilience Fund, turning a pollution penalty into flood-protection money for coastal towns [S2].
Preserves state authority to regulate or fee methane emissions separately, so the federal fee would be a floor, not a ceiling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that produce, gather, process, or transmit oil and gas and let methane escape above the small allowance; some of that fee would likely show up in energy prices, though much of it is avoidable by fixing leaks the companies are already losing money on.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies with leaky operations

drawbacks.text: Basin-level emissions estimates, done by satellite or air sampling, would be less precise than company-by-company measurement, so firms that follow the rules could be charged for leaks they did not cause unless they go through the protocol-validation opt-out process [S3].

The opt-out path depends on the Treasury Secretary validating each company's measurement protocol, which invites fights over whether a protocol is truly 'accurate and comprehensive' and could delay the fee for years [S3].
The $1,800-per-ton charge is high enough that some of it would likely be passed through to consumers in natural gas and oil prices, at least for companies that choose to pay rather than fix leaks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually consumer-friendly for a pollution fee: it exempts the first 0.2% of losses, so operators pay mainly for gas they are wasting and losing money on, and the bill's own findings say much of that waste can be eliminated at no net cost [S3]. The main honest objections are the precision of satellite-based basin measurements and the possibility that non-compliant companies pass their fees to customers; but the bill also leaves state and EPA regulation untouched [S3]. The bigger question is not design but support: it never gathered enough of it to get a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Natural Resources committees and to two of their subcommittees, and neither committee took any further action before the Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Deutch (D-FL) introduced the bill on June 23, 2021, with Rep. Charlie Crist (D-FL) as the only cosponsor [S3].

The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Natural Resources Committee; within a month it was passed down to the Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee and the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote followed, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers are better off because the $1,800-per-ton methane fee never advanced; the public got no new coastal resilience funding and no new federal lever to cut methane leaks. With only two House supporters and two committee referrals, the bill's failure is less a dramatic block than a quiet lack of traction in a Democratic-controlled House that chose not to move it [S4].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers, not coastal communities

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no party breakdown exists; both supporters were Democrats, and no Republican ever cosponsored the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers, processors, and pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill charges these companies $1,800 per ton for methane they release above a small allowance, with an escape hatch only for firms that measure their leaks publicly and stop routine venting and flaring [S3]. Because a large share of the waste can be captured at no net cost by the industry's own estimates, the fee mainly prices the emissions the industry would otherwise keep externalizing onto everyone through climate damage.

industries.industry: Methane detection and measurement technology firms
industries.note: The bill requires empirically determined, peer-reviewed emissions measurements — on the ground or by drone, airplane, or satellite — and validates company monitoring protocols, creating demand for exactly these services; the bill's findings highlight companies developing such technology [S3]. Their business grows only when emissions actually get measured and cut, so their interest runs with the public's here.

industries.industry: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation / coastal restoration sector
industries.note: The bill would transfer all fee revenue annually to this foundation for coastal resilience grants, making it the permanent federal channel for methane-fee money [S2]. Its role and funding would be locked in by the same bill that creates the revenue.
